subtopic_detail: Antibiotic selection in preterm prelabour rupture of membranes
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 33 year old woman in her third pregnancy at 32 weeks and 1 day. She reports a sudden gush of clear fluid four hours ago followed by continued dampness.

Speculum examination shows a pool of clear liquor in the posterior fornix with no bleeding and a closed cervix. She has no contractions and no uterine tenderness. Her temperature is normal, her white cell count and C reactive protein are within normal limits, and the cardiotocograph is reassuring with a baseline of 138. Her group B streptococcus status is unknown and her low vaginal swab has just been sent. She had betamethasone commenced one hour ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 86, BP 116/70, RR 15, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.8, foetal heart rate baseline 138
data_table.Examination: Speculum: pool of clear liquor, cervix closed, no bleeding, no uterine tenderness
data_table.Investigations: White cell count and C reactive protein within normal limits; cardiotocograph reassuring; low vaginal swab pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic management?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin with clavulanate for ten days alongside expectant inpatient management
options.rationale: Amoxicillin with clavulanate is the near pair that must be avoided in this setting because it is associated with a significant increase in neonatal necrotising enterocolitis (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Guideline

options.text: Oral erythromycin for ten days alongside expectant inpatient management with surveillance
options.rationale: Erythromycin prolongs the latency period, reduces chorioamnionitis and reduces neonatal morbidity in preterm prelabour rupture of membranes without the necrotising enterocolitis signal seen with other agents (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Guideline

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin now and continuing until delivery for group B streptococcus cover
options.rationale: Intrapartum prophylaxis is given once labour starts or delivery is planned rather than continuously during expectant management, which would select resistant organisms over weeks (Source: RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus Guideline

options.text: No antibiotics with daily observations, and treatment commenced only if maternal fever develops
options.rationale: Withholding antibiotics loses the demonstrated reduction in chorioamnionitis and the prolongation of latency that allows corticosteroids to take effect (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Guideline

options.text: Oral metronidazole for seven days with repeat vaginal swabs performed at weekly intervals
options.rationale: Metronidazole targets anaerobic vaginosis and has not been shown to improve outcomes after membrane rupture, and it does not cover the organisms driving ascending infection here (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Guideline

explanation.summary: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes before 37 weeks is managed expectantly to about 37 weeks provided there is no chorioamnionitis, no foetal compromise, no significant bleeding and no established labour. Ten days of erythromycin is standard because it prolongs latency and reduces neonatal morbidity, while amoxicillin with clavulanate is specifically avoided after trial data showed increased necrotising enterocolitis. Antenatal corticosteroids are given as they would be for any threatened preterm birth in the eligible gestational window. Surveillance for chorioamnionitis relies on maternal temperature, pulse, uterine tenderness, liquor character and cardiotocograph rather than on serial inflammatory markers, which perform poorly in this setting.
key_points: Erythromycin for ten days is the recommended antibiotic after preterm membrane rupture
Amoxicillin with clavulanate is avoided because of increased neonatal necrotising enterocolitis
Expectant management continues to about 37 weeks if surveillance stays reassuring
Group B streptococcus prophylaxis is given intrapartum rather than throughout expectant care
explanation.pearls: Serial C reactive protein has poor sensitivity and specificity for chorioamnionitis after membrane rupture; a rising maternal pulse with foetal tachycardia is the earlier and more reliable warning pair.

sources.label: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Guideline
RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus Guideline

subtopic_detail: Iron deficiency anaemia from excessive cow milk intake in a toddler
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing an 18 month old boy whose mother is worried he looks pale and has become fussy and less interested in playing over two months. He walks and has around ten words.

He drinks about 1200 mL of cow milk daily from a bottle and eats very little solid food, refusing meat entirely. He has no diarrhoea, no blood in his nappies and normal growth along the 50th centile for weight and height. He was born at term and has no family history of anaemia or bleeding disorders. His coeliac serology, taken with total immunoglobulin A, is negative and his stool testing shows no occult blood. His blood film shows hypochromic microcytic red cells with anisocytosis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, BP 92/56, RR 26, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Investigations: Blood film: hypochromic microcytic red cells with anisocytosis; coeliac serology with total immunoglobulin A negative; faecal occult blood negative
data_table.Blood tests: Haemoglobin 84 g/L (105-135); mean cell volume 62 fL (73-85); ferritin 6 micrograms/L (15-150); C reactive protein within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Transfuse packed red cells and recheck the full blood count before discharge from the day unit
options.rationale: Transfusion is reserved for cardiovascular compromise or a much lower haemoglobin, and this child is well perfused with a haemoglobin that will respond to oral therapy (Source: RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency).

options.text: Intravenous iron infusion arranged at the paediatric day unit within the next two weeks
options.rationale: Parenteral iron is for malabsorption, intolerance of oral therapy or failure to respond, none of which has yet been established in an untreated child (Source: RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency).

options.text: Oral iron supplementation with cow milk reduced below 500 mL daily and iron rich solids introduced
options.rationale: Excessive cow milk causes iron deficiency by displacing iron rich solids, inhibiting absorption and causing occult enteric blood loss, so treatment pairs oral iron replacement with the dietary correction that prevents recurrence (Source: RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency).

options.text: Dietary advice alone with cow milk reduced below 500 mL daily and repeat blood testing in three months
options.rationale: Diet alone corrects the cause but replenishes stores far too slowly when the ferritin is already 6 micrograms per litre with symptomatic anaemia (Source: RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency).

options.text: Haemoglobin electrophoresis before any treatment to exclude an underlying thalassaemia trait
options.rationale: Electrophoresis is the near pair investigation for microcytosis, but a ferritin of 6 micrograms per litre already establishes iron deficiency, and iron deficiency itself distorts electrophoresis results (Source: RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency).

explanation.summary: Iron deficiency is the commonest nutritional deficiency in Australian toddlers and excessive cow milk intake is the usual mechanism, operating through three routes at once: displacement of iron rich foods, calcium and casein inhibition of iron absorption, and occult gastrointestinal blood loss from cow milk protein induced enteropathy. Treatment always pairs replacement with correction of the cause, because iron given without reducing milk intake produces relapse once the course ends. Oral therapy is given for three months beyond haemoglobin normalisation to refill stores rather than stopped when the haemoglobin recovers. Neurodevelopmental effects of iron deficiency in this age group may be only partly reversible, which is the reason for treating rather than observing.
key_points: Cow milk above about 500 mL daily is the usual cause in Australian toddlers
Ferritin below 15 micrograms per litre confirms deficiency once inflammation is excluded
Continue oral iron for three months after the haemoglobin normalises to refill stores
Iron deficiency distorts haemoglobin electrophoresis, so treat first and test later if microcytosis persists
explanation.pearls: Recheck the full blood count after four weeks of oral iron and expect a haemoglobin rise of at least 10 g/L; failure to reach that mark points to adherence problems, ongoing blood loss or a wrong diagnosis rather than a need for a higher dose.

sources.label: Australian Medicines Handbook Children's Dosing Companion

subtopic_detail: Autism recognition in an adult woman presenting as treatment resistant anxiety
stem:
You are the psychiatrist seeing a 24 year old graphic designer referred with anxiety that has not responded to sertraline, escitalopram or venlafaxine at adequate doses and durations over three years.

She describes exhaustion after workplace social events, and says she rehearses conversations beforehand and copies phrases from colleagues. Fluorescent lighting and the office air conditioner noise are intolerable to her, and she has worn the same brand of clothing since childhood because of the fabric. Her mother reports she lined up her toys by colour and had one intense interest at a time throughout primary school. Her anxiety is worst when routines change at short notice, and she has no history of trauma, panic attacks or compulsions.

data_table.Examination: Mental state: anxious, limited spontaneous eye contact, precise and detailed speech, no thought disorder
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, thyroid function and iron studies within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Augment the current antidepressant with low dose aripiprazole and review in six weeks
options.rationale: Augmentation treats the presumed anxiety disorder as the primary problem, yet the lifelong sensory, social and routine features suggest the wrong condition is being treated (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Anxiety Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Anxiety Disorders

options.text: Refer for a structured multidisciplinary autism diagnostic assessment with a developmental history
options.rationale: Lifelong sensory sensitivity, social camouflaging, insistence on sameness and circumscribed interests warrant formal diagnostic assessment, which in Australia requires a structured tool plus a corroborated developmental history (Source: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia).
source_refs: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia

options.text: Diagnose borderline personality disorder and refer for dialectical behaviour therapy skills
options.rationale: There is no affective instability, no identity disturbance, no self harm and no pattern of unstable relationships, and this misdiagnosis is a documented pathway for autistic women (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Personality Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Personality Disorders

options.text: Commence a stimulant trial for possible inattentive presentation attention deficit disorder
options.rationale: Inattention is not the reported problem and stimulants will not address sensory intolerance or social exhaustion, although the two conditions do co occur and can be screened after diagnosis (Source: Australian Evidence Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD).
source_refs: Australian Evidence Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Increase the venlafaxine to the maximum tolerated dose and add graded exposure therapy
options.rationale: A fourth serotonergic escalation after three adequate trials repeats a failed strategy, and exposure work aimed at social anxiety does not target sensory or routine driven distress (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Anxiety Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Anxiety Disorders

explanation.summary: Autistic women are diagnosed later and less often than men, largely because camouflaging behaviours mask the social features while the resulting exhaustion presents as anxiety or depression. Repeated antidepressant non response in a person with lifelong sensory sensitivity and need for sameness should prompt a developmental reformulation rather than another pharmacological step. Australian practice requires a multidisciplinary assessment with a structured instrument and a corroborated developmental history rather than a single clinic impression. Diagnosis matters practically because it changes the therapeutic approach, opens funded supports and reduces the risk of iatrogenic harm from repeated medication trials.
key_points: Camouflaging delays autism diagnosis in women and presents as anxiety, exhaustion or depression
Three failed adequate antidepressant trials should prompt diagnostic review, not a fourth escalation
Australian diagnosis needs a structured tool plus corroborated developmental history
Borderline personality disorder is a common misdiagnosis in this group and requires affective instability and identity disturbance to be present
explanation.pearls: Distinguishing autistic sensory intolerance from social anxiety turns on whether distress occurs when alone with the stimulus; social anxiety requires an audience, sensory intolerance does not.

sources.label: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia
RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Anxiety Disorders
RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Personality Disorders
Australian Evidence Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

subtopic_detail: Empirical antibiotic choice in acute pyelonephritis requiring admission
stem:
You are the emergency registrar admitting a 34 year old woman with 24 hours of fever, rigors and right loin pain. She has vomited three times this morning and cannot keep down oral fluids.

She is not pregnant on a beta human chorionic gonadotrophin test, and has had no urinary catheter, hospitalisation or antibiotic exposure in the last six months. She has no known drug allergies and takes no regular medication. She has right renal angle tenderness on examination. Her urine dipstick shows nitrites and leucocytes and a specimen has gone for culture. Her creatinine and potassium are within normal limits and a bedside ultrasound shows no hydronephrosis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112, BP 104/64, RR 22, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 39.1
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick nitrites and leucocytes positive; urine culture pending; bedside ultrasound no hydronephrosis
data_table.Blood tests: White cell count 16.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); creatinine and potassium within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Oral trimethoprim 300 mg once daily for fourteen days with early general practitioner review
options.rationale: She is vomiting and cannot absorb oral therapy, and trimethoprim resistance rates in Australian urinary isolates are too high for empirical use in systemic infection (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Oral nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily for seven days with oral rehydration in the department
options.rationale: Nitrofurantoin is the classic near pair error here because it concentrates in urine but does not achieve therapeutic renal parenchymal or serum levels, so it never treats pyelonephritis (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for seven days once the vomiting has been controlled
options.rationale: Fluoroquinolones are reserved in Australia for resistant isolates or specific allergy situations because of resistance stewardship and tendinopathy and neuropathy risk (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin with a loading dose calculated on actual body weight and level monitoring
options.rationale: Vancomycin covers Gram positive organisms and misses the Gram negative Enterobacterales that cause the overwhelming majority of pyelonephritis (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Intravenous gentamicin with intravenous amoxicillin and review at 48 hours with the culture
options.rationale: Australian empirical therapy for pyelonephritis requiring admission is intravenous gentamicin plus amoxicillin, covering Enterobacterales and enterococci, with narrowing once susceptibilities return (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Acute pyelonephritis is distinguished from lower urinary tract infection by systemic features such as fever, rigors and loin pain, and this distinction determines both the antibiotic and its route. Agents that concentrate in urine without achieving tissue levels, notably nitrofurantoin and fosfomycin, are effective for cystitis and useless for upper tract disease. Australian empirical therapy uses gentamicin with amoxicillin, with a single daily gentamicin dose and level monitoring if therapy continues beyond 48 hours. Imaging is reserved for those failing to improve at 48 to 72 hours, for suspected obstruction, or for a known stone history, since obstruction with infection is a urological emergency.
key_points: Fever, rigors and loin pain define upper tract infection and change the drug and the route
Nitrofurantoin and fosfomycin never treat pyelonephritis despite good urinary concentrations
Empirical Australian therapy is intravenous gentamicin plus amoxicillin
Reimage at 48 to 72 hours if there is no clinical improvement
explanation.pearls: Gentamicin in this setting is given as a single daily dose of 4 to 7 mg/kg using ideal body weight, and a trough level is only required if therapy extends beyond 48 hours or renal function is impaired.

subtopic_detail: Group B streptococcus prophylaxis with severe penicillin allergy
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the birth suite with a 30 year old woman in her first pregnancy at 39 weeks and 2 days, now in established labour at 5 cm dilated with intact membranes.

Her routine 36 week low vaginal swab grew group B streptococcus. Antibiotic susceptibility testing was not requested on that isolate and the laboratory advises that the specimen is no longer available. Her allergy history records anaphylaxis to amoxicillin at age 22 requiring adrenaline and an overnight admission. She has no other allergies. Her observations and the cardiotocograph are reassuring and delivery is anticipated within the next four to six hours.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 94, BP 118/74, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.9, foetal heart rate baseline 140
data_table.Investigations: 36 week low vaginal swab positive for group B streptococcus; susceptibility testing not performed and isolate unavailable; cardiotocograph reassuring

lead_in: What is the most appropriate intrapartum antibiotic?

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin with adrenaline and resuscitation equipment available at the bedside
options.rationale: Rechallenge with a beta lactam after documented anaphylaxis is not acceptable practice when effective alternatives exist, regardless of what monitoring is available (Source: RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus Guideline

options.text: Intravenous cefazolin, since cross reactivity between penicillins and cephalosporins is uncommon
options.rationale: Cefazolin is appropriate for a low severity penicillin allergy such as a delayed rash, but documented anaphylaxis places her in the high severity group where cephalosporins are avoided (Source: RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus Guideline; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).
source_refs: RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus Guideline

options.text: Intravenous clindamycin, which is the standard alternative agent in severe penicillin allergy
options.rationale: Clindamycin is used only when the isolate has been confirmed susceptible, and Australian group B streptococcus resistance to clindamycin is high enough that empirical use is unreliable (Source: RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus Guideline

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin given as an infusion and repeated at the recommended dosing interval
options.rationale: With documented anaphylaxis to a penicillin and no clindamycin susceptibility result available, vancomycin is the recommended intrapartum agent because group B streptococcus remains uniformly susceptible to it (Source: RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus Guideline; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).
source_refs: RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus Guideline

options.text: Intravenous erythromycin given as an infusion and repeated at the recommended dosing interval
options.rationale: Macrolide resistance in group B streptococcus is common and erythromycin achieves poor foetal levels, so it is not recommended for intrapartum prophylaxis (Source: RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus Guideline

explanation.summary: Intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis for group B streptococcus aims to have at least four hours of maternal therapy before delivery, which is when neonatal colonisation falls most. Benzylpenicillin is first line, with cefazolin substituted for low severity penicillin allergy such as an isolated delayed rash. High severity allergy, meaning anaphylaxis, angioedema, respiratory distress or a severe cutaneous adverse reaction, requires clindamycin only where susceptibility is proven and otherwise vancomycin. This is why laboratories should be asked for clindamycin susceptibility whenever a screening swab from a penicillin allergic woman grows the organism, since that single request determines whether vancomycin can be avoided later.
key_points: Aim for at least four hours of intrapartum therapy before delivery
Benzylpenicillin first line, cefazolin for low severity allergy
Clindamycin only when the isolate is confirmed susceptible
Vancomycin where allergy is severe and susceptibility is unknown
explanation.pearls: Request clindamycin susceptibility at the time the 36 week swab is collected for any penicillin allergic woman; without it the default in labour becomes vancomycin, which needs an infusion time that a rapid labour will not allow.

sources.label: RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus Guideline

subtopic_detail: Imaging choice for suspected developmental dysplasia of the hip at six weeks
stem:
You are the general practitioner performing a six week check on a baby girl. She was born at 38 weeks by caesarean section for breech presentation at term and her mother's sister was treated in a harness as an infant.

The baby is feeding well and gaining weight along the 50th centile. On examination the Ortolani and Barlow tests are both negative today, but abduction of the left hip in flexion is limited to 55 degrees compared with 80 degrees on the right, and there is an extra skin crease on the left thigh. Leg lengths appear equal with the knees flexed and the feet together. Her neonatal hip examination in the postnatal ward was documented as normal and her tone and reflexes are normal today.

data_table.Examination: Ortolani and Barlow negative; left hip abduction in flexion 55 degrees versus 80 degrees on the right; asymmetric left thigh skin crease; Galeazzi test negative
data_table.Investigations: Neonatal hip examination documented as normal in the postnatal ward

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Plain anteroposterior radiograph of the pelvis arranged today with orthopaedic review of the films
options.rationale: The femoral head is largely cartilaginous before about four to six months, so radiography is unreliable at six weeks and is the wrong modality for this age (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

options.text: Repeat clinical examination at the six month immunisation visit with no imaging in the interim
options.rationale: Delaying to six months forfeits the window in which harness treatment is highly effective, and limited abduction is a recognised sign of an established dislocation (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

options.text: Commence a Pavlik harness now and arrange orthopaedic review within the following two weeks
options.rationale: Harness treatment is prescribed and monitored by orthopaedics on the basis of confirmed imaging, and applying one to a normal hip carries a risk of avascular necrosis (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of both hips under sedation to define the position of the femoral heads
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging requires sedation, is not the standard first line test in infancy, and adds nothing over ultrasound at this age (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

options.text: Ultrasound of both hips arranged now with orthopaedic referral if the acetabular indices are abnormal
options.rationale: Ultrasound is the investigation of choice under about four to six months because it images the cartilaginous femoral head, and limited abduction with a breech history and a positive family history mandates imaging despite negative provocative tests (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

explanation.summary: Developmental dysplasia of the hip is screened for clinically at every infant check, and Australian practice adds selective ultrasound for babies with risk factors regardless of examination findings. The principal risk factors are breech presentation in the third trimester, a first degree family history and female sex, and breech alone is an indication for imaging even with a normal examination. Ortolani and Barlow tests lose sensitivity after about three months because a dislocated hip becomes fixed rather than reducible, at which point limited abduction, asymmetric thigh creases and apparent leg length inequality become the leading signs. Ultrasound is used under four to six months and radiography thereafter, once the femoral head ossific nucleus has appeared.
key_points: Ultrasound is the imaging modality under about four to six months, radiography after
Breech presentation and a first degree family history each independently warrant imaging
Ortolani and Barlow lose sensitivity after about three months as the hip becomes fixed
Limited abduction and asymmetric creases are the signs of an established dislocation
explanation.pearls: Ultrasound performed before six weeks of age generates false positives from normal neonatal ligamentous laxity, so a scan for risk factors alone is scheduled at six weeks rather than in the first days of life.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip
Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care neonatal hip guidance

subtopic_detail: First line therapy selection in established post traumatic stress disorder
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 32 year old delivery driver eight months after a highway collision in which a passenger died. He re experiences the crash as intrusive images several times daily, avoids the highway entirely, sleeps four hours a night and startles at car horns.

He has taken no medication, drinks two standard drinks weekly and uses no other substances. He works reduced hours and his employer is supportive. He has no suicidal ideation, head injury or prior psychiatric history. He asks what treatment gives him the best chance of getting back on the highway.

data_table.Examination: Mental state: anxious, hypervigilant to noise in the corridor, no psychotic features, no cognitive impairment
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function and thyroid function within normal limits

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg daily and titrate over four weeks according to response
options.rationale: Medication is recommended when trauma focused therapy is declined, unavailable or has failed, or where severe comorbid depression prevents engagement, none of which applies here (Source: Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Acute Stress Disorder, PTSD and Complex PTSD).
source_refs: Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Acute Stress Disorder, PTSD and Complex PTSD

options.text: Prescribe a short course of temazepam nightly to restore sleep before starting therapy
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are specifically advised against in post traumatic stress disorder because they impair the extinction learning that trauma focused therapy depends on (Source: Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Acute Stress Disorder, PTSD and Complex PTSD).
source_refs: Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Acute Stress Disorder, PTSD and Complex PTSD

options.text: Arrange single session psychological debriefing focused on retelling the collision narrative
options.rationale: Single session debriefing has no benefit and may worsen outcomes, and it is a different intervention from the structured multi session trauma focused therapies that do work (Source: Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Acute Stress Disorder, PTSD and Complex PTSD).
source_refs: Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Acute Stress Disorder, PTSD and Complex PTSD

options.text: Refer for trauma focused cognitive behavioural therapy delivered over eight to twelve sessions
options.rationale: Individual trauma focused psychological therapy, either trauma focused cognitive behavioural therapy or eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing, is the first line recommendation for adults with post traumatic stress disorder ahead of pharmacotherapy (Source: Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Acute Stress Disorder, PTSD and Complex PTSD).
source_refs: Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Acute Stress Disorder, PTSD and Complex PTSD

options.text: Commence prazosin at night for nightmares and review the sleep pattern in six weeks
options.rationale: Prazosin targets nightmares specifically and is an adjunct considered after first line therapy is underway, not an initial treatment for the whole syndrome (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Australian guidance places individual trauma focused psychological therapy ahead of medication for adults with post traumatic stress disorder, with roughly eight to twelve sessions as the standard course and more where there is multiple or prolonged trauma. Pharmacotherapy is reserved for those who decline or cannot access therapy, who have not responded, or whose comorbid depression is too severe to allow engagement. Benzodiazepines are actively discouraged because they blunt the emotional processing that exposure based work relies on. Recovery is measured functionally, and returning to avoided situations such as the highway is a core therapy target rather than an incidental outcome.
key_points: Trauma focused cognitive behavioural therapy and eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing are equal first line
Sertraline, paroxetine, fluoxetine and venlafaxine are the medication options when therapy is not the chosen route
Benzodiazepines are advised against because they impair extinction learning
Single session debriefing after trauma is not recommended and may cause harm
explanation.pearls: Prazosin for trauma related nightmares starts at 1 mg at night and needs a lying and standing blood pressure check before each increase, as first dose hypotension is the main reason patients stop it.

sources.label: Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Acute Stress Disorder, PTSD and Complex PTSD

subtopic_detail: Osteoporosis pharmacotherapy selection with impaired renal function
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 72 year old woman four weeks after she sustained a T12 vertebral compression fracture while lifting a shopping bag. The fracture was confirmed on plain radiography and her back pain is now settling with simple analgesia.

She is postmenopausal since age 51, has never smoked, and takes no corticosteroid. Her corrected calcium, phosphate and parathyroid hormone are within normal limits and her serum 25 hydroxyvitamin D is 68 nmol/L after supplementation. A myeloma screen is negative. Her bone mineral density shows a lumbar spine T score of minus 2.8. Her renal function has been stable at this level for two years.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 70, BP 132/78, RR 14, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Investigations: Lumbar spine T score minus 2.8; T12 vertebral compression fracture on radiography; myeloma screen negative
data_table.Blood tests: eGFR 28 mL/min/1.73m2; corrected calcium, phosphate and parathyroid hormone within normal limits; 25 hydroxyvitamin D 68 nmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological treatment?

options.text: Subcutaneous denosumab six monthly with calcium and vitamin D supplementation continued
options.rationale: Denosumab is cleared by the reticuloendothelial system rather than the kidney and needs no dose adjustment, making it the antiresorptive of choice when eGFR falls below 30 mL/min/1.73m2 (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology; Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Oral alendronate 70 mg weekly taken fasting with calcium and vitamin D supplementation continued
options.rationale: Oral bisphosphonates are renally cleared and are contraindicated once eGFR falls below 30 to 35 mL/min/1.73m2, which is the single discriminator between this and the correct agent (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Intravenous zoledronic acid five milligrams annually with calcium and vitamin D continued
options.rationale: Zoledronic acid shares the same renal clearance limitation as oral bisphosphonates and is contraindicated below an eGFR of 35 mL/min/1.73m2 (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Calcium 1200 mg and colecalciferol 1000 international units daily as the sole ongoing therapy
options.rationale: Supplementation is adjunctive and does not reduce refracture risk after a minimal trauma vertebral fracture, which mandates specific antiresorptive or anabolic therapy (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Subcutaneous teriparatide daily for eighteen months with calcium and vitamin D continued
options.rationale: Teriparatide is an anabolic option for very severe or treatment refractory disease and carries restricted Australian subsidy criteria that this presentation does not yet meet (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

explanation.summary: A minimal trauma vertebral fracture establishes osteoporosis regardless of bone mineral density and mandates pharmacological therapy, since the risk of a further fracture in the following year is substantially raised. Agent selection is driven by renal function, by whether an oral route is tolerated, and by prior treatment. Bisphosphonates are renally cleared and become unsuitable below an eGFR of roughly 30 to 35 mL/min/1.73m2, whereas denosumab is not renally cleared. Secondary causes must be excluded before committing to therapy, which is why myeloma screening, calcium, parathyroid hormone and vitamin D belong in the initial workup.
key_points: A minimal trauma vertebral fracture diagnoses osteoporosis irrespective of T score
Bisphosphonates are contraindicated below an eGFR of about 30 to 35 mL/min/1.73m2
Denosumab is not renally cleared and requires no dose adjustment
Correct vitamin D and calcium before starting any antiresorptive to avoid hypocalcaemia
explanation.pearls: Denosumab must never simply be stopped, because bone turnover rebounds and multiple vertebral fractures can follow within a year; a bisphosphonate is given at the time of cessation to consolidate the gains.

subtopic_detail: First line therapy for heavy menstrual bleeding with iron deficiency
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 41 year old woman who describes flooding through a super tampon hourly on her heaviest two days and passing clots the size of a fifty cent coin. Her cycles are regular at 28 days and this pattern has been present for two years.

She has completed her family and does not want further children, and would prefer to avoid an operation. She has no intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding, pelvic pain or dyspareunia. Her cervical screening test six months ago was negative for human papillomavirus. Her transvaginal ultrasound reports a normal uterus with no fibroid, no polyp and an endometrial thickness of 6 mm. Her thyroid function and coagulation screen are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 118/72, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound: normal uterus, no fibroid or polyp, endometrial thickness 6 mm; cervical screening test negative for human papillomavirus
data_table.Blood tests: Haemoglobin 98 g/L (115-165); ferritin 8 micrograms/L (30-200); thyroid function and coagulation screen within normal limits

options.text: Oral tranexamic acid taken on the heaviest days of each cycle with oral iron replacement
options.rationale: Tranexamic acid reduces blood loss by around a third and is a reasonable second choice, but it provides no contraception and is less effective than the recommended first line option (Source: RANZCOG Heavy Menstrual Bleeding Guideline).

options.text: Oral mefenamic acid taken through the bleeding days of each cycle with oral iron replacement
options.rationale: Non steroidal anti inflammatory agents reduce loss by only about 20 to 30 per cent and are the least effective of the medical options offered here (Source: RANZCOG Heavy Menstrual Bleeding Guideline).

options.text: Referral for endometrial ablation at the next available gynaecology outpatient appointment
options.rationale: Ablation is effective but is a surgical procedure she has asked to avoid, and it is offered after medical therapy has failed rather than before it is tried (Source: RANZCOG Heavy Menstrual Bleeding Guideline).

options.text: A combined oral contraceptive pill taken continuously without a hormone free interval and oral iron
options.rationale: The combined pill is effective and does provide contraception, but it reduces menstrual loss less than the intrauterine option and carries thrombotic risk that rises after age 40 (Source: RANZCOG Heavy Menstrual Bleeding Guideline).

options.text: A levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine system inserted in the practice with oral iron replacement
options.rationale: The levonorgestrel intrauterine system reduces menstrual blood loss by 70 to 90 per cent, outperforms all oral medical options, provides contraception and avoids surgery, which matches every stated preference here (Source: RANZCOG Heavy Menstrual Bleeding Guideline).

explanation.summary: Heavy menstrual bleeding is defined by its effect on the woman rather than by a measured volume, and structural assessment is directed by symptoms and risk rather than performed reflexively in every case. Where the uterus is structurally normal, the levonorgestrel intrauterine system is first line because it reduces blood loss more than any oral agent and preserves fertility and the uterus. Tranexamic acid and non steroidal anti inflammatories are useful for women who want cycle specific treatment without hormones, and the combined pill suits those wanting cycle control plus contraception. Iron deficiency is treated in parallel rather than after the bleeding is controlled, because ferritin recovery takes months and symptoms of deficiency respond before the haemoglobin does.
key_points: Levonorgestrel intrauterine system is first line for heavy bleeding with a structurally normal uterus
It reduces blood loss by 70 to 90 per cent, more than any oral agent
Tranexamic acid reduces loss by about a third and gives no contraception
Treat iron deficiency concurrently rather than waiting for bleeding control
explanation.pearls: Warn about irregular spotting for the first three to six months after insertion of a levonorgestrel intrauterine system; unwarned bleeding is the commonest reason for early removal, and most women become oligomenorrhoeic or amenorrhoeic by twelve months.

subtopic_detail: Preventer initiation threshold in childhood asthma
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 7 year old boy who has attended three times this year for wheeze. He has a written asthma action plan and uses salbutamol through a spacer.

Over the last three months he has needed salbutamol three times most weeks for chest tightness during football training, and wakes coughing about twice a month. He has had no oral corticosteroid course and no emergency presentation this year. His inhaler technique with the spacer was checked by the practice nurse today and was correct, and his mother confirms he has no exposure to tobacco smoke at home. He has eczema and allergic rhinitis, both well controlled. His spirometry today shows a forced expiratory volume in one second of 88 per cent predicted.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 100/62, RR 20, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Chest clear on auscultation today; no accessory muscle use; growth along the 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: Spirometry: forced expiratory volume in one second 88 per cent predicted; inhaler technique with spacer verified as correct

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence a low dose inhaled corticosteroid preventer through the spacer and review in four weeks
options.rationale: Reliever use on more than two days per week or night waking more than twice a month indicates poor control and triggers preventer therapy, with low dose inhaled corticosteroid the first line agent in this age group (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook).

options.text: Commence oral montelukast at night as the preventer of choice given his coexisting allergic rhinitis
options.rationale: Montelukast is less effective than inhaled corticosteroid as a preventer and carries a neuropsychiatric warning, so it is a second line option rather than first choice (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook).

options.text: Commence a combination inhaled corticosteroid and long acting beta agonist inhaler through the spacer
options.rationale: Combination therapy is the near pair but is reserved for children whose symptoms persist despite an adequate trial of inhaled corticosteroid alone, which has not yet been tried (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook).

options.text: Increase salbutamol to a regular four times daily schedule through the spacer and review in one month
options.rationale: Regular short acting beta agonist use does not treat the underlying airway inflammation and is associated with worse asthma outcomes (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook).

options.text: Commence a five day course of oral prednisolone and continue reliever therapy as currently prescribed
options.rationale: Oral corticosteroid treats an acute exacerbation rather than establishing long term control, and there is no exacerbation today (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook).

explanation.summary: Asthma control in children is assessed over the preceding four weeks using daytime symptoms, reliever use, night waking and activity limitation, and any one feature out of range means the asthma is not well controlled. Reliever use on more than two days per week is the threshold most often crossed and is the usual trigger for starting a preventer. Before escalating therapy the four checkable causes of apparent treatment failure are reviewed: inhaler technique, adherence, ongoing trigger exposure and comorbid conditions such as rhinitis or obesity. Low dose inhaled corticosteroid remains the first line preventer in school aged children, with a review at four to six weeks to confirm response before any step up.
key_points: Reliever use on more than two days per week signals poor control and triggers preventer therapy
Check technique, adherence, triggers and comorbidities before escalating
Low dose inhaled corticosteroid is first line preventer in school aged children
Combination inhalers are reserved for persistent symptoms despite adequate corticosteroid
explanation.pearls: Review any new preventer at four to six weeks, since inhaled corticosteroid takes two to four weeks to reach effect; escalating earlier because of no immediate benefit is the commonest reason children end up on combination therapy they do not need.
